Liittovaltion tuomari on asettanut kiireellisen väliaikaismääräyksen, joka kieltää Donald Trumpin presidentinhallintoa painostamasta Yhdysvaltojen vaaliviranomaisia.
Asiasta uutisoi muun muassa CNN. Yhdysvaltojen välivaalit käydään tiistaina. Trump on toistuvasti vihjaillut, että vaaleissa voisi esiintyä vilppiä.
Tuomari Trina Thompson kertoo, että oikeusministeriö ja sisäisen turvallisuuden ministeriö eivät voi vaatia minkään osavaltion vaaliviranomaisia erottelemaan äänestyslippuja, poistamaan äänestäjiä vaaliluettelosta tai keskeyttämään äänten käsittelyä, kun tuomarin asettama määräys on voimassa. Määräys lakkaa 16. marraskuuta.
– Vaikka vastaajat väittävät toimien olevan suunnattu ulkomaalaisten laittoman äänestämisen estämiseen, ne todennäköisesti häiritsevät vaalien järjestämistä ja riistävät äänioikeuden laillisilta äänestäjiltä, Thompson sanoi paikallista aikaa perjantai-iltana.
Lisäksi Thompson vaatii, että presidentinhallinto tiedottaa häntä kaikista vaatimuksista päästä käsiksi äänestyslipukkeisiin tai vaalimateriaaleihin.
CNN:n mukaan presidentinhallinto on käynnistänyt kiistellyn operaation, jossa verrataan äänestäjäluetteloita liittovaltion henkilörekistereihin. Näin sisäisen turvallisuuden ministeriö on luonut listoja ihmisistä, joilta epäillään puuttuvan Yhdysvaltojen kansalaisuus, CNN kirjoittaa.
Vaaliviranomaisten mukaan listat ovat epäluotettavia ja sisältävät myös Yhdysvaltojen kansalaisia, CNN kuvailee.
Thompsonin käsittelemä tapaus tuotiin Kalifornian piirioikeuteen, jonka CNN kertoo olevan ”vasemmalle kallellaan”. Kanteen nostivat ammattiliitot ja kansalaisoikeusjärjestöt.
Thompson puolestaan on demokraattipresidentti Joe Bidenin nimittämä tuomari.
Aiemmin kalifornialaistuomari David Carter esti oikeusministeriön vaatimuksen eritellä yli 20 000 äänestäjän äänestysliput. Ministeriö väitti, että kyse on muiden kuin Yhdysvaltojen kansalaisten äänistä.
Yhdysvaltojen osavaltiot ovat vastuussa vaalien järjestämisestä alueillaan.

sources.news_title: Federal Judge Shuts Down Trump’s Threats to Prosecute Election Officials
sources.text:

Days after the US Department of Justice threatened election officials in all 50 states with possible prosecution unless they preserve election records — the latest push by the Trump administration to cast doubt on the validity of the upcoming midterm elections — a federal judge on Friday ordered the DOJ to reach out to the officials again, this time to rescind the threat.
The DOJ must contact the state and local officials who received warnings this week and inform them that the “threats of prosecution to election officials and workers… have been enjoined,” said District Judge Trina Thompson in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.
Thompson ordered officials with the Trump administration to stop demanding that election workers remove voters from rolls, sequester ballots cast by people the White House has claimed are ineligible to vote due to being noncitizens, and refuse to issue ballots to people who have been included on the administration’s error-riddled lists of residents whom it says have voted illegally.
“Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in plaintiffs’ favor,” said Thompson.
The ruling was handed down in connection with a lawsuit filed by the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), and other groups.
Protect Democracy, part of the coalition that sued, called the threat “yet another attempt designed to shake Americans’ confidence in the election results and undermine our electoral process.”
Patrick Moran, president of AFSCME, said Thompson’s ruling and the temporary restraining order she issued were “a resounding win for the election workers who make our democracy happen and for all Americans’ freedom to vote.”
“We applaud the court for granting a temporary restraining order protecting election workers from unlawful prosecution simply for following the law and forbidding the administration from interfering with the lawful administration of elections,” said Moran. “Now, our nation’s nonpartisan election workers, many of them AFSCME members, can continue to do their jobs, and our elections can continue to proceed freely and fairly.”
With President Donald Trump’s approval rating at a historic low and Republicans facing widespread disapproval of the illegal war on Iran they’ve supported, healthcare cuts they voted for, and violent mass deportation operations they’ve funded, the White House has approached the midterms with a laser focus on sowing doubt about the results before the elections are completed.
The DOJ demanded confidential voter roll data from states across the country last year, pushing the baseless claim that the lists were rife with the names of noncitizens who would be illegally permitted to vote. The administration has been rebuffed by dozens of officials.
In response, the Department of Homeland Security and DOJ have used commercially available data and federal records to cobble together their own lists of voters they say have cast ballots illegally. The results of the effort have included a list of 185 people in Nevada, all of whom were proven to be citizens, and a list of 28 immigrants in California whom federal officials said were suspected of voting before they became naturalized citizens — representing about .0001% of all registered voters in the state.
The administration has also pushed for the certification of Alaska’s election results to be blocked, citing the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot — one clearly labeled as the incumbent Republican senator, the other not — and on Thursday, sent the threatening letters to election officials across the country.
Earlier this week, Judge David Carter in the US District Court for the Central District of California said that the administration’s threats “must stop,” throwing out the DOJ’s attempt to force the state to sequester ballots cast by 20,000 people officials claimed were not citizens.
“DOJ tried to bully election workers with threats and intimidation,” Norm Eisen, co-founder of Democracy Defenders Action, said Saturday. “Last night, a federal court shut it down. We and our partners are fighting to protect elections in the court of law.”

sources.text:
US Judge Bars Threats to Election Staff
Published Saturday, October 31, 2026, 11:45 a.m. ET · Source: federal court orders, Emerson College Polling, University of Florida Election Lab, Polymarket
Three days before Election Day, federal judges are drawing a line around who may pressure the people who count America’s votes. On Friday a US judge ordered the Justice Department, the nation’s top federal law-enforcement agency, to stop threatening election officials over disputed ballots. It is the latest turn in our 2026 US midterm elections coverage.
This story is part of our coverage of the 2026 US midterm elections. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide.
Key Facts
- Order: a US judge in California barred federal officials from threatening local vote counters, through November 16.
- Alaska: the Justice Department wants ballots naming a second “Sullivan” set aside, and certification halted if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
- Early voting: nearly 49.6 million ballots were cast by Friday evening.
- Prediction markets: Polymarket prices a Democratic Senate win at 71.5% and a Democratic House win at 94.5% (as of 11:22 a.m. ET, October 31).
What The California Judge Ordered
On Friday, October 30, US District Judge Trina Thompson of the Northern District of California issued a temporary restraining order, a short-term court order that freezes a dispute until a fuller hearing. It bars the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from threatening criminal prosecution to coerce state and local election officials, where the pressure rests only on claims that voters are ineligible.
The order also stops both agencies from demanding that officials in any state set ballots aside, purge voter lists or halt ballot processing. It runs through November 16, and labor unions and civil-rights groups brought the case.
Why The Appeals Court Matters Too
The same day, the Ninth US Circuit Court of Appeals, the federal appeals court for California and other Western states, again refused the Justice Department’s request to pause a ruling on more than 20,000 California ballots. The 2–1 decision found the department had not met its burden of proof.
It was the second rejection in a week. The administration argues that a data-matching programme flags voters who may not be eligible, while election officials say such matches can be wrong.
The Alaska Fight Over Two Sullivans
In Alaska, the Justice Department asked a federal court to set aside all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a second candidate who shares a name with the Republican senator. It also asked the court to block certification of the result if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
US District Judge Sharon Gleason set a fast schedule, with replies due at noon Alaska time on Saturday (4 p.m. ET). A ruling could follow once that briefing closes. Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate nominee, denies any role in recruiting the second Sullivan and called the claims “offensive”.
How Many Americans Have Already Voted
The University of Florida Election Lab, which tracks early voting, counted 49,564,545 ballots cast early by Friday evening.
The final Emerson College Polling national survey, taken October 24–26 among 1,000 likely voters, put Democratic House candidates ahead 52% to 42%. Its credibility interval, a margin-of-error measure, is plus or minus 3 percentage points.
What Prediction Markets Say
- Senate control: Democratic Party 71.5%, Republican Party 28.5% on Polymarket, with about US$13.3 million traded.
- House control: Democratic Party 94.5%, Republican Party 5.5% on Polymarket, with about US$33.8 million traded.
These prices are bets, not polls, and they were read at 11:22 a.m. ET on October 31. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.
What It Means For US Readers
Election Day is Tuesday, November 3. Expect results to arrive in stages, because states set their own polling hours and count mail, provisional and challenged ballots on their own timetables. A close Senate race may stay open for days if courts are still ruling.
What Is Not Known
It is not known whether the Alaska judge will set ballots aside or limit certification. Nor is it clear whether the Justice Department will appeal the California order.
No one can yet say whether the early-vote surge favours either party. Official results are final only when each state finishes counting.
Sources
Federal court orders (N.D. Cal., Ninth Circuit, D. Alaska); Emerson College Polling national survey, October 24–26, 2026; University of Florida Election Lab; Polymarket.

Frequently Asked Questions

She barred the Justice Department and Homeland Security from threatening election officials over disputed ballots. The order runs through November 16.
When is Election Day?
Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Polling hours differ by state.

Judge blasts Trump team for threatening election workers in latest rebuke to midterm plans
Election workers and voting rights groups accused DOJ of launching an intimidation campaign over alleged noncitizen voters

A federal judge has blocked Donald Trump’s administration from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution for processing ballots — thwarting the government’s last-ditch attempts to toss out votes before Election Day.
The temporary restraining order prevents the Department of Justice and Homeland Security from demanding state and local election officials stop processing or setting aside ballots in the president’s crusade against alleged noncitizen voters.
“One of the hallmarks of a fair election is the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear or intimidation,” California District Judge Trina Thompson wrote Friday night.
“Free exercise of the right to vote is a core tenet of our democracy,” she added. “Election Day is around the corner. Ballots have already been issued. Americans have already begun voting. Workers have already begun processing ballots. Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.”
The ruling follows a lawsuit from unions representing election workers and civil rights groups who accused the administration of trying to illegally “intimidate” them with threats of criminal prosecution in the weeks before high-stakes midterm elections, with the balance of power in Congress at stake.
According to Judge Thompson, “high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.”
“Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” she wrote.
Friday night’s order arrived hours after a federal appeals court in the state blocked the administration’s efforts to sequester 20,000 ballots, which another judge warned would “wreak havoc” on elections in the state.
That legal battle could soon head to the Supreme Court next if the administration wants to keep fighting, with just days left before Election Day on Tuesday.
Appellate court judges said the administration’s attempts to set aside ballots while voting is already underway could “jeopardize” midterm elections and disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.
That 2-1 decision marks the third straight loss for the administration in its efforts to block ballots from alleged noncitizen voters in the state.
“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the court’s majority wrote on Friday.
The court has “major concerns” that the administration’s attempts to seize control of the state’s election process will risk “disenfranchisement of eligible voters” and could put the “entire tabulation process in jeopardy,” judges wrote.
Federal law mandates a “quiet period” 90 days before an election to ensure voters aren’t wrongly disenfranchised without enough time to make corrections.
But the Justice Department launched an unprecedented effort to seize ballots and prevent states from certifying votes with just days left before midterm campaigns come to an end.
The Justice Department is also trying to press officials in Washington state to sequester ballots from at least 400 people the administration has accused of being noncitizens.
The Trump administration is also embroiled in an increasingly volatile attempt to block the certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate results if Trump’s preferred candidate loses.
Election experts and voting rights groups said a court’s intervention in the election workers’ case is a relief for the small army of people who run the nation’s elections.
“This decision is a resounding win for the election workers who make our democracy happen and for all Americans’ freedom to vote,” said Patrick Moran, president of the American Federation Of State County And Municipal Employees, among the unions suing the Trump administration.
Election workers can now “continue to do their jobs, and our elections can continue to proceed freely and fairly,” he added.

sources.text:
Donald Trump’s Department of Justice has been ordered to stop threatening to prosecute or launch investigations into election workers—following weeks of aggressive tactics intended to root out ineligible voters that the court said were likely “interfering with the lawful administration” of the 2026 midterms.
On Friday, a federal judge issued the temporary restraining order after a number of labor groups brought forward a lawsuit against the DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). As summarized in the court order, the agencies' officials were accused of engaging in a campaign to “intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.”
“Free exercise of the right to vote is a core tenet of our democracy. It requires safeguarding to ensure full participation and public trust in our elections. Election Day is around the corner,” Judge Trina Thompson of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, wrote in her opinion.
Read More on News
“Ballots have already been issued. Americans have already begun voting. Workers have already begun processing ballots. Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.”
When approached for comment, the DOJ told Newsweek the decision demonstrated a "two-track system of justice," and said it would be "reviewing the order and evaluating all options.”
“The judge issued an order against the federal government without even waiting to hear from the United States, while in other cases the Department’s own urgent election claims are delayed by judges until after Election Day," spokesperson Kiersten Pels said.
What Is the Case About?
The case concerns the administration’s push to stamp out what president Trump has described as “rampant” voter fraud and noncitizen voting, a political priority that has already prompted tighter proof-of-citizenship verification requirements in the leadup to the 2026 elections.
As outlined in Friday’s emergency order, plaintiffs brought the case because of their belief that “in the lead-up to the election, high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.”
“Specifically, Defendants have threatened the criminal prosecution of state and local election workers if they process and count ballots using procedures required by federal and state law,” the plaintiffs said.
Over the past few weeks, the DOJ has sent out letters—in some cases “delivered by armed DHS officials”—to election officials across the U.S., warning them of investigations and criminal penalties that will follow if they fail to preserve records or process ballots of those the government alleges are ineligible to vote.
“On October 13, 2026 Defendants sent letters demanding that the California Secretary of State and Los Angeles County Registrar California officials sequester the ballots of approximately 20,000 registered California voters whom Defendants ‘believe’ are ‘likely’ non-citizens,” the order reads. “When the State and Los Angeles County refused, Defendants sued them in the Central District of California.”
“Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” District Judge Thompson wrote upon granting the temporary restraining order.
What Does the Order Do?
Thompson said that the defendants’ actions likely violate the 1965 Voting Rights Act, the Constitution’s Elections Clause and its Fifth and Tenth Amendments. While not a final judgment on the original lawsuit, Friday’s order temporarily blocks some of the government’s election-enforcement efforts.

sources.news_title: Federal Judge Blocks Trump Administration From Warning Election Officials of Criminal Penalties Over Disputed Ballots
sources.text:
A federal judge has ordered the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security to stop informing election workers of potential prosecution for processing ballots from voters the administration suspects are noncitizens, while a separate appeals court ruling rejected a request to set aside approximately 20,000 California ballots.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
A federal judge in California issued an emergency order Friday, Oct. 30, prohibiting the Trump administration from informing state and local election officials of criminal prosecution for processing ballots belonging to registered voters whose citizenship the federal government has questioned.
U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson of the Northern District of California ruled that the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security had likely violated federal election law by pressuring officials to halt ballot processing or separate ballots associated with individuals identified by federal investigators as potentially ineligible voters.
The ruling came just four days before the Nov. 3 midterm elections and followed Justice Department letters demanding that California election officials cooperate with federal citizenship verification efforts.
According to NBC News’ reporting on the decision, Thompson granted a temporary restraining order after labor unions and civil rights organizations challenged the administration’s demands.
The lawsuit was brought by the Service Employees International Union, the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, the League of United Latin American Citizens and the NAACP.
In her eight-page order issued Oct. 30, Thompson described the federal government’s conduct as an effort to pressure election workers who were carrying out their responsibilities under existing election procedures.
“In the lead-up to the election, high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election,” the order stated, recounting the allegations presented by the plaintiffs.
The court found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims that the administration’s conduct violated the Voting Rights Act’s prohibition against intimidation, threats or coercion in connection with voting.
“Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” the order stated, describing the plaintiffs’ allegations.
Thompson prohibited federal officials from pressuring election workers to stop processing ballots solely because the administration alleges that the registered voters who submitted them are ineligible.
The order also bars demands that election officials remove specific registered voters from voter rolls, refuse to issue them ballots or segregate their ballots based solely on the federal government’s allegations concerning their eligibility.
Federal officials are additionally prohibited from threatening criminal prosecution against election workers who refuse those demands or process ballots in compliance with state and federal election laws.
The temporary restrictions extend through 5 p.m. Nov. 16, nearly two weeks after Election Day.
The judge also directed the Justice Department to disclose pending search warrant applications, grand jury subpoenas and other demands involving election materials or ballots connected to the government’s lists of suspected ineligible voters.
Federal authorities must notify state and local governments that previously received the disputed letters that the demands and prosecution threats contained in those communications have been temporarily prohibited.
The confrontation stems from an investigation conducted by federal immigration and law enforcement agencies into approximately 20,000 California voter registrations.
The Trump administration maintains that its investigators identified individuals who are likely noncitizens but remain registered to vote in federal elections.
Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Justice Department has argued that California officials must take appropriate steps to prevent ballots cast by ineligible individuals from being counted.
On Oct. 13, federal officials demanded that California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County election officials separate ballots associated with individuals on the government’s list until their citizenship could be verified.
When California officials refused, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit Oct. 15 seeking emergency court intervention.
The administration subsequently expanded its demands to election officials across California.
Federal prosecutors sent letters to officials in 57 of California’s 58 counties, warning about potential criminal liability for processing ballots belonging to individuals the government believes are ineligible.
A letter sent to San Bernardino County election officials Oct. 22 emphasized the federal prohibition against noncitizen voting.
“As you’re aware, federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections,” the letter stated.
“I write to seek your help to protect the integrity of the ongoing federal election.”
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli also identified more than 1,000 registered voters in San Bernardino County whom federal investigators classified as likely noncitizens.
“Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,” Essayli wrote.
The department sought access to nonpublic voter registration information, potentially including Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers and state identification records.
“That means sending us the nonpublic information associated with each suspected alien’s registration,” Essayli wrote.
The government also requested that ballots associated with individuals whose citizenship could not be confirmed be separated from other ballots.
“For individuals whom citizenship status cannot be confirmed, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate—not cancel—those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined.”
The administration argued that separating the ballots would preserve the opportunity to determine voter eligibility before the ballots were removed from their identifying envelopes and counted.
A social media post circulating during the dispute highlighted the government’s arguments about potential voter fraud and the consequences of counting ballots before citizenship verification is completed.
The Justice Department maintains that once a ballot is separated from its identifying envelope and incorporated into the vote count, election officials generally cannot determine how that particular voter voted.
Essayli criticized California’s refusal to follow the federal government’s requests.
“California election officials were given an opportunity to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls and to sequester ballots returned from suspected ineligible voters. They refused,” he said.
California officials disputed the accuracy of the federal list and argued that the proposed procedures could interfere with lawful voting.
The state maintained that the names identified by federal investigators had not been conclusively established as belonging to noncitizens and that some individuals on the list appeared to be eligible American voters.
A separate legal dispute over those ballots reached the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday.
In a 2-1 decision, the appellate panel rejected the Justice Department’s request to require California to set aside ballots associated with approximately 20,000 registered voters while their citizenship status was investigated.
The appeals court decision, reported by The Epoch Times, followed an earlier district court ruling denying the administration’s request for emergency relief.
Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez concluded that federal officials had not demonstrated sufficient grounds for the requested intervention.
The majority warned that forcing California to identify and separate thousands of ballots during an ongoing election could disrupt ballot processing and potentially prevent eligible citizens from having their votes counted.
The judges declined the administration’s “invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text.”
“If the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts,” the ruling stated.
The majority also agreed with the district court’s assessment of the practical consequences of separating individual ballots.
“As the district court found—and we discern no clear error—there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.”
Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented, arguing that the government’s request represented a reasonable effort to preserve disputed ballots until citizenship verification could be completed.
The appellate ruling did not establish that every individual identified by the Justice Department is eligible to vote. Instead, it addressed whether the government had demonstrated sufficient grounds for an emergency order requiring California to change its election procedures.
A second social media post discussing the court decisions addressed the administration’s attempt to prevent disputed ballots from being counted before verification.
The two Friday decisions involved separate lawsuits but addressed related questions about federal authority over election administration.
Thompson’s temporary restraining order specifically concerns threats, demands and potential criminal prosecution directed at election workers. The Ninth Circuit’s ruling addresses the government’s request for an emergency injunction requiring California to separate disputed ballots.
Neither decision changes the federal prohibition against noncitizen voting or prevents law enforcement from investigating credible allegations of election fraud through lawful procedures.
The dispute centers on whether federal authorities can compel state election officials to depart from established ballot-processing procedures based on allegations that particular registered voters lack citizenship.
In explaining the urgency of her order, Thompson emphasized that voting and ballot processing were already underway.
“Election Day is around the corner. Ballots have already been issued. Americans have already begun voting. Workers have already begun processing ballots. Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.”
The federal government must submit its response to the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction by noon Nov. 2. Thompson scheduled a hearing for Nov. 13, three days before the temporary restraining order expires.
California election officials may continue processing ballots under existing state and federal procedures while the lawsuits proceed, and the Justice Department’s allegations concerning the disputed voter registrations remain unresolved.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson's temporary restraining order, issued on a challenge brought by labor and civil-rights organizations, found that federal officials' efforts to pressure election administrators likely violated federal voting protections and exceeded the government's constitutional authority. Her order prohibits federal demands that ballots be set aside on the basis of ineligibility allegations alone, and bars threats of prosecution against workers who refuse those demands or who process ballots in accordance with state and federal law. "In the lead-up to the election," she wrote, "high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election." The order builds on an earlier finding by Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín that federal threats had already caused citizens to withdraw from electoral activity. The Justice Department has said enforcing election law is its responsibility and that it would not wait for a "more convenient time." Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg who shares a name with the two-term Republican incumbent, had been under way for several months and that a New York Times report suggesting Mary Peltola's campaign had been involved in recruiting him had produced "a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska." Heyman would not say what crimes were under investigation or who the targets were. It is highly unusual for the department to confirm the existence of a criminal investigation at all, and its longstanding practice has been to avoid public steps in the weeks before an election that could be read as an attempt to influence the result; a press conference asking voters for tips four days out is a departure that prosecutors of both parties would once have considered unthinkable.

Bryan Wilson asked the court to order Alaska to "preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary," and requested a decision by Monday. Sullivan has long denied running at Democrats' behest, and the DSCC denies involvement. Republican Gov. But it states the principle the Alaska court will now have to weigh on Monday, that the federal government may not use the threat of prosecution or the segregation of lawful ballots as an instrument against the officials who count them, and it was issued by a judge who had read the department's own letters. Whether the department can both obey that order in California and Washington and obtain the one it wants in Alaska is the question the weekend will not answer and Tuesday will make moot or urgent.

In issuing the temporary order, Thompson concluded that the plaintiffs were likely to show the administration’s actions violated the Voting Rights Act and exceeded federal authority under the Constitution, the Chronicle reported. Axios reported that the judge found election employees had been put at risk of prosecution for carrying out their work.
Other court decisions constrain election-related actions
The order came as the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals again rejected the administration’s request to block about 20,000 California ballots from voters it alleges are noncitizens. The Los Angeles Times reported that the panel said election administration authority rests with California and Congress, rather than the federal executive branch. The same panel had denied the request earlier in the week, following a separate rejection by a district judge.
In a separate case, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín barred DHS officers in nine states from field operations targeting people they know or reasonably suspect are U.S. citizens; the Ninth Circuit kept those restrictions in place through Election Day. NPR reported that Martínez-Olguín found the government’s use of incomplete, unreliable data and publicized arrests could discourage people from helping others exercise their voting rights. The appeals court also questioned the timing of the government’s actions, NPR reported.
Federal records demands and voter data disputes
The order comes amid federal requests for election records and voter data. The Justice Department sent letters to 29 states and Washington, D.C., seeking preservation of 2024 election records and voter data while warning of investigations, CNN reported. The department also sent letters to election officials in 57 of California’s 58 counties, according to CNN.
The Justice Department has said its election-related actions are intended to enforce federal laws against noncitizen voting. California’s registration and voter-list practices

County election officials also use the state’s VoteCal system for routine list maintenance, including checking for duplicate registrations and updating records when voters move.
